description: We are Orbital Harmonics, a student team making NASA Earth science accessible through sound. Our AETHER-9 Earth Information Jukebox turns satellite visuals into polyphonic music, 3D spatial audio, and spoken telemetry so blind and sighted explorers alike can hear our changing planet. By combining computer vision, Web Audio synthesis, and blind-first accessibility tools, we aim to turn silent climate and planetary data into an experience anyone can hear, explore, and feel.
summary:
AETHER-9 is a real-time, browser-native Earth Information Jukebox that transforms NASA’s Earth Information Center (EIC) visualizations into expressive, polyphonic music and 3D spatial audio.

Rather than converting pixels into harsh, random noise, AETHER-9 runs a live computer-vision scanline across four official NASA Scientific Visualization Studio (SVS) datasets—DYAMOND Global Carbon Dioxide (SVS 5196), Perpetual Ocean 2 (SVS 5425), Dixie Fire & Air Quality (SVS 4993/5533), and ISS Lightning & Polar Sea Ice (SVS 5011/5099)—plus any custom user-uploaded frame. It maps color hue to quantized musical scales (Phrygian, Lydian, Dorian, Pentatonic), pixel luminance to pitch and filter cutoff, and spatial edge turbulence to polyrhythmic FM pulses across a 4-voice Web Audio synthesizer.

Accessibility is built into every interaction. Blind and low-vision users can navigate the globe using keyboard arrow keys to trigger 3D left-to-right stereo panning, haptic feedback, and spoken Web Speech telemetry of exact coordinates and NASA metrics, or export any soundscape as a stereo .WAV file in one click.

Why it matters: Visual-only Earth science locks out millions of blind and low-vision citizens. AETHER-9 makes our planet’s vital signs audible, intuitive, and emotionally resonant for everyone.
details:
AETHER-9 (Auditory Earth Telemetry & Harmonic Resonance Engine) is a real-time, browser-native Earth Information Jukebox that translates satellite visualizations from NASA’s Earth Information Center (EIC) into polyphonic music and 3D spatial audio. While visual satellite maps show how our planet is changing, relying only on sight excludes blind and low-vision people and makes subtle patterns harder to notice. AETHER-9 solves this by turning every NASA EIC frame into a playable, accessible scientific instrument.

How It Works: Instead of playing pre-recorded tracks or turning pixels into harsh random noise, AETHER-9 scans NASA EIC frames at 60 FPS across 8 latitude bands (75°N to 75°S) and drives a 4-voice Web Audio synthesizer in real time:

  1. Color Hue to Musical Scale: Pixel colors lock onto musical scales so the data always sounds harmonious. Cool ocean blues trigger calm C Lydian chords, while intense carbon dioxide plumes and wildfires shift into urgent D Phrygian Dominant and A Dorian minor chords.
  2. Brightness (Luminance) to Pitch & Filter: Pixel brightness controls the lead melody pitch, deep planetary bass drone (55–110 Hz), and low-pass filter cutoff (220–4420 Hz). Bright thermal hotspots trigger high-register bell sparks.
  3. Swirling Edges (Sobel Gradient) to Rhythm: A 3x3 Sobel edge detector measures visual turbulence—like swirling Gulf Stream eddies or dense smoke plumes—and speeds up the FM arpeggiator rhythm.
  4. Longitude to 3D Headphone Panning: Left-to-right map position maps to 3D stereo panning (-1.0 Left to +1.0 Right), letting headphone users immediately hear whether an event is in the Western or Eastern Hemisphere.

Quick User Guide

  1. Select Dataset & Play: Press number keys 1–4 to switch between NASA Earth Information Center visualizations, and press Space to start or pause the real-time sonification.
  2. 3D Spatial Navigation: Use the keyboard Arrow Keys (↑, ↓, ←, →) to step the 3D sonic radar across Earth in 15° increments with headphone binaural stereo panning.
  3. Export Audio: Click Save .WAV in the control deck to download a 44.1 kHz, 16-bit PCM stereo audio file of the session.
  4. Upload Custom Frames: Drop any PNG or JPEG satellite image from NASA SVS or Earth.gov into the Open Science Uplink section to instantly turn its pixels into music.

Accessibility & Key Features:

  • Blind-First Keyboard Sonic Radar: Using only the arrow keys, blind users can step across Earth in 15-degree increments and hear pitched 3D sonar pings at every coordinate.
  • Spoken Voice Guide & Screen Reader Sync: Built-in Web Speech API and ARIA live regions read the exact latitude, longitude, NASA dataset value (such as ppm CO2 or m/s current speed), and pitch in Hertz out loud.
  • WCAG AAA High-Contrast Mode & Haptics: One-click yellow-on-black AAA contrast mode for low-vision users plus mobile vibration pulses.
  • Custom NASA Frame Upload & 1-Click .WAV Export: Users can upload any image from NASA SVS or Earth.gov for instant sonification and download a 44.1 kHz, 16-bit stereo .WAV audio file directly from the browser.

Tools, Languages & Software Used: Built with HTML5, CSS3, Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5 Canvas 2D API (real-time pixel extraction), Web Audio API (multi-oscillator synthesis, biquad filtering, 3D stereo panning, FFT spectrum analysis), Web Speech API, Web Vibration API, Tailwind CSS, and binary ArrayBuffer PCM .WAV encoding.

Super Intelligence (SI) Acknowledgement: Application code, procedural canvas shaders, and presentation graphics were developed with assistance from Google Gemini (Super Intelligence / LLM tool). All audio soundscapes are synthesized mathematically in real time via the Web Audio API.

The AETHER-9 project successfully bridges a critical accessibility and sensory gap in modern Earth science communication. By transforming complex, visual-only satellite telemetry from NASA’s Earth Information Center (EIC) and Scientific Visualization Studio (SVS) into real-time polyphonic music and 3D spatial audio, AETHER-9 redefines how humanity experiences planetary observation. Traditionally, dense climate datasets—ranging from global carbon dioxide plumes (SVS 5196) and oceanic boundary currents (SVS 5425) to wildfire perimeters (SVS 4993/5533) and polar ice shifts (SVS 5011/5099)—have been confined to visual charts and hyperwalls. This design paradigm inadvertently excludes blind and low-vision citizens while frequently causing cognitive overload for sighted users.

Our solution introduces a robust, zero-latency computer vision and Web Audio pipeline that operates entirely within the browser at 60 frames per second. By locking spectral hues to expressive harmonic scales (such as Lydian and Phrygian modes), mapping luminance to pitch registers, and utilizing 3D binaural headphone panning via keyboard navigation, AETHER-9 eliminates unmusical noise fatigue and converts raw data into an intuitive, emotional narrative of climate urgency.

Looking forward, AETHER-9 is primed for seamless integration into physical museum exhibits, science center kiosks, and multi-sensory STEM classrooms as part of NASA's expanding Earth Information Center DIY Toolkit on Earth.gov. By empowering educators, students, and blind explorers to independently investigate planetary change—and even upload custom satellite frames via the Open Science Uplink—this project proves that open-source science and universal design can unite to make our home planet's story accessible to everyone, everywhere.
